title: Giorgio Agamben
keyWorks: Stanzas: Word and Phantasm in Western Culture (1977)
summary: Giorgio Agamben (b. 1942) is an Italian philosopher and a reader of Aristotle, Benjamin, Heidegger and medieval theologians. He writes short, almost poetic essays about how the modern world takes away our time, our attention and our free use of things — and how we can take them back. His key words are “profanation” (returning things to free use), “inoperativity” (liberation from the obligation to produce) and the “potential not to” (the freedom not to do what you are able to do).
onEmotions: Agamben doesn’t write textbooks about feelings, but his ideas shed a great deal of light on them. He observes that modern people are constantly captured by “apparatuses” — devices and arrangements (from schedules to the smartphone) that steer desires and behavior. Many of our heavy states — tiredness, overload, anxiety — are bound up with the demand to be always producing and always switched on. Agamben proposes not escape but “inoperativity” (Italian inoperosità): not laziness, but the capacity to suspend the obligation to deliver results and to see life as a possibility rather than a task. For him, a person is defined not only by what they can do but also by what they can not do — and in this “not” lie dignity and freedom.

anxiety.text: “The time is short,” Paul writes to the Corinthians, and Agamben spent years reading those few words closely. When you are anxious, your thoughts run ahead, trying to live through everything that might happen in advance — and that is exhausting. In The Time That Remains, reflecting on the letters of the apostle Paul, Agamben distinguishes two ways of living time. One is an endless line along which we chase the future. The other is “the time that remains”: the contracted time we actually have, the present we live in rather than wait for. If we carry Agamben’s thought further, anxiety lives entirely in the first kind of time — a time that never arrives. There is no need to chase it away. But from time to time you can come back to the second: to this hour, this day, where the future has not yet taken the present from you.
anxiety.practice: Rest your palm on the table and feel how solid it is: this is your “time that remains.” Name one worry and ask whether it belongs to this hour. If not, make a gesture with your hand as if moving it to the edge of the table.

fear.text: “My age, my beast, who will be able to look into your eyes?” — with these lines by Mandelstam Agamben explains what being contemporary means. Fearing what is unclear and threatening is natural. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben writes that you can only truly see your own time if you don’t look away from its darkness, not just from its lit-up places. And he adds: this takes courage. Agamben would probably say that fear is often tied to our being afraid to look directly at what is dark. But the courage he speaks of is not fearlessness; it is the capacity to stay with what frightens you, without squeezing your eyes shut and without panicking. You don’t have to defeat fear all at once. You can try looking at it a little more closely — and discover that the darkness has contours.
fear.practice: Turn off the light or close your eyes and look into the darkness for a minute without turning away — like Agamben’s contemporary. Then name your fear in one precise sentence: what contours does this darkness have?

sadness.text: Medieval physicians explained melancholy by an excess of black bile. Sadness is still often asked to justify itself, though it has no need to. In his early book Stanzas, Agamben reconsiders the medieval idea of melancholy, long regarded as something like a vice. He shows that melancholy is bound up not with indifference but with desire: a person is sad because their desire is attached to something out of reach, and they go on holding on to it. It turns out that your sadness is not emptiness but a form of faithfulness to what is dear to you. Sadness keeps a connection with what has slipped away. That doesn’t mean you have to stay in it forever. But you can treat it with respect: your capacity to love and to desire lives in it.
sadness.practice: Take in your hands an object connected with what you are sad about — or picture it. Hold it for a minute, the way one holds something dear, and say quietly: “I am keeping this.”

grief.text: Agamben retells a Hasidic story in The Fire and the Tale: the descendants forgot the place in the forest, the fire and the prayer of the Baal Shem, but the story stayed with them. Grief needs time, and not all of it has to be remembered. In The Time That Remains, following Walter Benjamin, Agamben reflects on “the unforgettable.” Some lives and events, he writes, remain unforgettable even if no one in particular remembers them: what they ask of us is not so much to be remembered as to remain with us. What matters to Agamben here is this: what you have lost goes on belonging to the world, even when memory fades or pain makes remembering unbearable. You don’t have to hold everything in memory by effort in order to stay faithful. What was lost remains part of the world — and part of you — on its own.
grief.practice: Tell someone — or yourself, aloud — one short story about the person or thing you have lost. Not a whole life, just one scene: as in the Hasidic tale, the story can be enough.

loneliness.text: For Aristotle a friend is “another self,” and in his essay “The Friend” Agamben adds: friendship is a shared sensing of the sheer fact that the other exists. Loneliness hurts, and it is not your fault. In The Coming Community, Agamben reflects on what a community of people might be like if it weren’t based on obligatory belonging — to a nation, a class, a group, “our own kind.” He speaks of “whatever” being: a person is valuable not because they have the right qualities but because they are such as they are. It seems that loneliness is often born of the feeling that we have to meet certain conditions in order to be accepted. But the genuine community he dreams of doesn’t require a pass. You already belong to the world — not by merit, but simply because you exist.
loneliness.practice: Go outside or to a window and look at the passers-by as “whatever” beings: none of them had to pass a test to be here. Neither did you.

anger.text: A cat chases a ball of yarn as if it were a mouse — Agamben loves this image of play that frees a thing from its old purpose. Anger is a strong, honest feeling, and there is often a real injustice behind it. In Profanations, Agamben describes how many things in the modern world end up removed from free use: time, space, language, the body are turned into resources that someone else controls. He calls returning things to people “profanation.” In other words, anger often flares up where something has been taken from you — your time, your voice, your right to decide. Understanding this means not just seething but seeing exactly what you want to take back into your own free use. Then anger becomes not an explosion but a pointer.
anger.practice: Tell a friend, or yourself aloud, what exactly was taken from you — time, voice, the right to decide. Then say in one sentence: what do I want to take back into free use?

shame.text: “Where can I go to get away from myself?” — Agamben believes this silent question is the very heart of shame. It is very hard to bear. In Remnants of Auschwitz, reflecting on the hardest testimonies of the twentieth century, Agamben, following Emmanuel Levinas, describes shame as the feeling of being delivered over to yourself, unable to hide from yourself. For Agamben, shame is not a sign of being rotten but something that reveals the very way of being human: we are at once those who act and those exposed to another’s gaze. Agamben might point out that shame speaks of your openness, not your worthlessness. You can live through this feeling without turning it into a verdict on yourself.
shame.practice: Press your cool palms to your face and hold them there until your breathing evens out. Then tell yourself: “This shame says that I am open, not that I am bad.”

guilt.text: Kafka’s Josef K. is arrested though he “had done nothing wrong” — and in his essay “K.” Agamben suggests that K. brought the trial against himself. Guilt shows that it matters to you how you acted. But Agamben offers an important distinction. In Remnants of Auschwitz, he writes that the concepts of guilt and responsibility come from law, while ethics is something else: not a trial of yourself but, as in Spinoza, a teaching about the happy life. Following this line, endless self-accusation turns life into a court case in which you are both the accused and the prosecutor. That doesn’t mean actions don’t matter. But the ethical question is not “how guilty am I?” but “how do I want to live now?” This question opens the future, while the trial only keeps returning you to the past.
guilt.practice: Say aloud — to yourself or to someone close — not “how guilty am I?” but “how do I want to live after this?” And give one answer, also aloud.

envy.text: The Latin quodlibet, “whatever,” sounds to Agamben not like indifference but like “such as it pleases”: something loved together with all its properties. Envy hurts, especially when it seems that others have what you don’t. In The Coming Community, Agamben reflects on what makes a person valuable. Usually we judge by properties: talents, successes, looks. Agamben suggests otherwise: value lies in “suchness” — in a person being exactly as they are, with all their properties, yet not reducible to any one of them. In this light, envy always compares properties. But your value is not the sum of your properties, and it can’t be measured against someone else’s. You are not a set of qualities slightly fewer than someone else’s, but the one and only way of being yourself.
envy.practice: Imagine all your properties — talents, successes, looks — set aside like clothes on a chair. What remains? Stay for a minute with this “such as you are,” which has nothing to be compared with.

emptiness.text: “The noonday demon” — that is what monks called the despondency that struck in the hottest hour, when the day seemed to stand still. When nothing brings joy and you don’t even feel like wanting, it is very heavy. In Stanzas, Agamben reflects on the medieval notion of acedia. It was considered a sin of sloth, but Agamben offers another reading: a person in acedia is not indifferent; their desire is still alive, but it is directed toward something that has become unreachable. It follows that even in emptiness there lives a hidden desire — it simply hasn’t found its way. Emptiness is not your absence but a waiting. There is no need to force interest into flame. You can simply acknowledge: somewhere inside, something is still reaching out.
emptiness.practice: Say aloud the first thing that would come if you could want anything at all — even if it is strange. You don’t need to do anything with the answer: it is enough to hear that desire is still reaching out.

confusion.text: In Latin, in-fans means “one who does not speak,” and on this word Agamben builds a whole book about the infancy of experience. Confusion comes when words and familiar explanations stop working, and it is deeply uncomfortable. In Infancy and History, Agamben reflects on “infancy” in a special sense — the state before language, when we can’t yet name what we are experiencing. For him, this is not only a stage of life that has passed but a dimension a person returns to again and again: every time a new experience begins, we first find ourselves “without words.” If we carry Agamben’s thought further, confusion is such a return to the infancy of experience. It is uncomfortable, but new understanding is born from it. There is no need to rush to explanations — words will come after the experience.
confusion.practice: Look around the way an infant who doesn’t yet know words would: for a minute, simply notice colours, sounds and movement without naming them. The words can wait.

fatigue.text: Do we rest only so that we can work again? Agamben suspects this very arrangement wears us out. Your tiredness is real, and it doesn’t mean you aren’t trying hard enough. In the essay “The Hunger of an Ox,” from the collection Nudities, Agamben reflects on the Sabbath and the feast. A feast, he writes, is not merely a break from work but a special state in which ordinary activities become “inoperative”: we eat not to restore our strength but for the sake of eating itself; we walk not to get somewhere but simply to stroll. Agamben calls this inoperativity (inoperosità) and sees in it not laziness but liberation from the obligation to produce. Agamben would probably say that your tiredness is the voice of the part of you that wants not another break for the sake of work, but time that owes nothing to anyone.
fatigue.practice: Hold a five-minute Sabbath: take a walk with no purpose — not for errands, not for steps, just to walk. If you feel like stopping, stop.

boredom.text: A tick once lived eighteen years without food in a Rostock laboratory, as if suspended — Agamben recalls the case in The Open on his way to boredom. Boredom can be agonizing, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. Then he turns to Heidegger’s reflections on “profound boredom.” In it, according to Heidegger, the things around us seem to refuse to occupy us — and in this very refusal a person first notices that their life is not just a set of activities but an open possibility. Agamben develops this thought: boredom brings us to the edge of habitual behavior, where we sense that we could be otherwise. It turns out that boredom is not empty time but a time when the familiar has stopped holding us. You don’t have to drown it out; you can listen: what possibility is opening up in this “nothing is interesting”?
boredom.practice: For five minutes, stay in your boredom like that suspended tick: no phone, no tasks. Notice the moment the familiar stops holding you — and what comes instead.

joy.text: What does a child playing with an old key have in common with an adult in a moment of joy? Agamben would answer: both have freed a thing from its purpose for a while. Joy is worth living fully. In “In Praise of Profanation,” from the collection Profanations, Agamben writes about children’s play: a child takes any object — an old toy car, a document, a key — and turns it into a plaything, freeing it from its former purpose. Play, for Agamben, returns things to a free, light kind of use. Agamben would probably say that joy often resembles such play: for a while, things and activities stop being obligations and become simply something to enjoy. Joy doesn’t have to be earned or justified. You can let yourself play with the moment without turning it into a task.
joy.practice: Pick up any object nearby — a spoon, a lid, a pencil — and play with it for a minute like a child: let it become something other than what it is for. Laugh if it is funny.

love.text: What do you love someone for? Agamben suspects there is no right answer — and that this is exactly the secret of love. Tenderness is one of the most important feelings we have. In The Coming Community, Agamben writes that love is not directed at particular qualities of the beloved: their beauty, intelligence or kindness. But neither does it disregard them: the lover wants the other with all their properties — such as they are. Agamben calls this “whatever” being: not “it doesn’t matter which,” but such that all of it matters. It seems that love is the experience of another person in their “suchness.” And perhaps it is in love that we ourselves first feel accepted not for something, but whole.
love.practice: Tell someone you love — or tell them in your mind — about one thing you love in them not for its usefulness or merit, but simply because it is them.

quote.text: The coming being is whatever being.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

gratitude.text: In 1964 Agamben, a twenty-two-year-old student, played the apostle Philip in Pasolini’s The Gospel According to St. Matthew — a role that simply fell to him. Gratitude is a warm feeling in which the world briefly seems generous. In the essay “Magic and Happiness,” from Profanations, Agamben writes that true happiness is never a reward for merit: what we achieve through our own efforts brings a different kind of joy, while happiness comes like magic — as a gift, unearned. In other words, gratitude is the recognition of such a gift. You have received something that could not have been earned — and it is not a debt to be repaid but a reason for joy. Gratitude frees you from the bookkeeping of merit: you can simply accept the good without asking whether you deserve it, and be glad that the world is sometimes generous.
gratitude.practice: Say a short “thank you” aloud, addressed not to a person but to chance: for one good thing you didn’t earn — it simply happened.

hope.text: A halo, Agamben writes in the last chapter of The Coming Community, adds nothing to the saint — it is only a slight trembling at the edges. Hope is especially precious in hard times. In the same book he retells a parable that Walter Benjamin heard from Gershom Scholem: in the world to come, everything will be as it is now, just a little different. There is no need to destroy everything and build it anew — a small displacement that changes everything is enough. Agamben might point out that hope doesn’t require the promise of a complete transformation. It can rest on tiny changes that are possible already: a slightly different way of looking, a slightly different place for things. The better may not be far away — it may be just a small shift away. Such hope is modest, but that is exactly why it is hard to take away.
hope.practice: Move one thing in the room — a cup, a chair, a book — a few centimetres. See how everything around shifts just a little, and think what similar tiny displacement is possible today.

nostalgia.text: In Self-Portrait in the Studio, Agamben, now past seventy, goes through the photographs and objects on the walls of his study — and each one opens a door into the past. Nostalgia is a tender longing, with nothing shameful in it. In Stanzas, Agamben offers a bold thought about melancholy: it is not simply a reaction to a real loss but a remarkable capacity of the imagination to make something unreachable present — even if as something lost. Following this line, nostalgia often longs not only for what was, but for what never was exactly as it is remembered. This is not deception but the creative work of memory: this is how we hold on to what is dear to us. You can value nostalgia as a way of keeping a connection with what shaped you, without demanding that the past come back.
nostalgia.practice: Like Agamben in his study, choose one old photograph or object and look at it for two minutes. Ask: what exactly am I keeping in it — a place, a time, or a feeling?

craving.text: Agamben describes how, within a few years, people with phones in their hands changed their gestures — their walk, their posture, even the way they look. A craving can be very strong, and its coming is not your fault. In the essay “What Is an Apparatus?”, Agamben describes devices and arrangements — from schedules to the smartphone — that capture our gestures and desires. In this light, a craving is a moment when your desire is being steered by something from outside: a habit, a device, a substance. Agamben proposes “profanation” — returning things and gestures to free use. You might try noticing the craving without giving in to it right away: it rises and falls, like a wave. Each such pause is a small return of freedom to yourself.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, put a hand on your belly and for a few minutes watch it rise and fall like a wave. Ask: who is doing the wanting right now — me, or the habit?

quote.text: If to consecrate (sacrare) was the term that designated the removal of things from the sphere of human law, to profane meant, conversely, to return them to the free use of men.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

addiction.text: What does it mean to use a thing rather than be used by it? Agamben puts this question to the whole modern world. Addiction is not a moral failure. It is a loop that has become fixed and organized a life around itself, and getting out of it is hard. In “In Praise of Profanation,” Agamben distinguishes “use” from “consumption”: to use a thing is to have a free, living relationship with it; to consume means the thing is swallowed up, and the person is captured by its logic. It follows that addiction is a place where free use has turned into compulsion. It isn’t about weakness of character: Agamben shows that much of modern life is designed to capture us. Getting your freedom back is a long road, and you don’t have to walk it alone.
addiction.practice: Think of someone you could say one honest sentence to about your habit — a person close to you or a mutual-help group. First say it aloud to yourself, to hear how it sounds.

hangover.text: Who are you — last night, or this morning? Agamben would answer: neither on its own, but the way you live. The morning after can be very hard — feeling unwell, shame, gaps in memory — and still it is no reason to punish yourself. In The Coming Community, Agamben writes that a person is not the sum of separate acts but a “manner,” a way of being: how they live, not only what they have done. If we carry Agamben’s thought further, last night is not the final definition of you. Your way of being includes this morning too: how you treat yourself now. There is no need to put yourself on trial. You can simply get through this morning gently, taking care of yourself the way you would care for someone close to you.
hangover.practice: Do one simple thing slowly, as a gesture of care: wash your face with cool water, open a window, make the bed. Do it the way you would look after someone close to you.

euphoria.text: What do you do when a door you weren’t looking for suddenly swings open? Agamben would probably say: first, just stand on the threshold. When everything seems possible, it is a vivid, powerful state, and there is no need to spoil it. In the essay “Magic and Happiness,” Agamben writes that true happiness comes not as a deserved reward but as magic — unexpectedly, unearned. It seems that euphoria feels exactly like this: as if a door you weren’t looking for had opened. Agamben also reminds us that human power includes the “potential not to” — not everything that is possible in this moment has to be done right away. This doesn’t cool the euphoria; it lets you live it more fully: to enjoy what has opened up without turning every sense of possibility into an obligation.
euphoria.practice: Stand on a threshold for a minute — literally, in a doorway — feeling how much is possible right now and deciding nothing. Let possibility stay possibility.

crash.text: After the feast comes Monday — but Agamben asks whether the feast is really so separate from ordinary days. A sharp drop after a high is very unpleasant, and no wonder it is felt so keenly. In the essay “The Hunger of an Ox,” Agamben writes that a feast is not a separate time set against everyday life but a special way of living ordinary activities: eating, talking, walking not for their usefulness but just because. It turns out that the comedown is often sharper when the feast seems like an exception and everyday life like a gray duty. But you can gradually carry the festive into ordinary life. The drop doesn’t mean everything good is over. It can become a time when you learn to find grains of celebration in the simplest things.
crash.practice: Do one everyday thing — wash a cup, make some tea — slowly and festively, as on a holiday, not for its usefulness.

panic.text: In “Notes on Gesture,” Agamben recalls how in 1886 the physician Gilles de la Tourette studied human walking from footprints on a roll of paper — step by step. When panic hits — terror, a pounding heart, the feeling that something irreparable is about to happen — it is very frightening. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. There Agamben also writes of the gesture as an action that produces nothing and leads nowhere — pure movement. What matters to Agamben here is this: in panic the mind feverishly tries to understand what is happening and paints a catastrophe. Simple gestures with no goal — an out-breath, touching the floor, looking at an object — help you return to your body without solving anything. You don’t need to understand anything. It is enough to wait out the wave.
panic.practice: Place your feet on the floor and feel the support, like a footprint on paper. Take a few slow breaths, each out-breath a little longer than the in-breath, and make one simple gesture with no goal: run your palm along your knee and name aloud three objects around you.

dread.text: In 1966 the young Agamben sat in Heidegger’s seminar at Le Thor in Provence, listening to a man who never looked away from the question of nothingness. “What is all this for,” the sense of an abyss — this is one of the hardest feelings. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben offers an unexpected view of darkness. He points out that, according to neurophysiology, darkness is not simply the absence of light: there are special cells in the eye that actively “produce” it. Seeing darkness is also an activity. It seems that your dread is not blindness but a way of seeing what others don’t notice. It takes courage, but there is dignity in this way of looking too. The darkness you are looking at is not the end of meaning but the place where the question of meaning begins.
dread.practice: Write down your “what for” in one sentence — not to answer it, but to see its outline, the way the eye makes out shapes in the dark.

quote.text: The contemporary is he who firmly holds his gaze on his own time so as to perceive not its light, but rather its darkness.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

fomo.text: Can you be late for the “now”? Agamben thinks it is impossible even to arrive there on time. It hurts to feel that life is happening somewhere you are not. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben reflects on fashion. Fashion, he writes, always lives in a “now” that can’t be grasped: as soon as you are “in fashion,” you are already almost out of it. In other words, the fear of missing out is a chase after this elusive “now,” which by its very nature can’t be caught. But Agamben also says something else: the truly contemporary person is one who doesn’t fully coincide with their time and keeps a little distance. Being “not there” is not a failure but the condition for seeing clearly what is going on.
fomo.practice: Put your phone face down and spend five minutes “out of fashion,” not knowing what is happening right now. Notice that life is going on here too.

sleepless.text: The monks whose rules Agamben studied lived by a schedule even at night: vigils, prayers at the appointed hour. We, on the contrary, need the night free of all duties. When you can’t sleep, it is agonizing, and night thoughts feel heavier than daytime ones. Agamben might point out that at three in the morning the mind keeps working — trying to solve problems, draw conclusions, make plans — as if even the night were obliged to deliver results. Agamben calls liberation from the obligation to produce “inoperativity” (inoperosità). The night hours don’t have to be productive, or even rest in the strict sense. You don’t have to solve your thoughts; you can simply let them go by without taking part. This isn’t a cure for insomnia, but it removes an extra weight — the feeling that you have to do something with this night.
sleepless.practice: Whisper to yourself, like a night prayer in reverse: “Tonight I don’t have to solve anything.” Repeat it slowly a few times, on the out-breath.

betrayal.text: When the ancient Greeks swore an oath, they called the gods as witnesses — and at once added a curse in case it was broken. When a trust that seemed solid collapses, it wounds deeply. In The Sacrament of Language: An Archaeology of the Oath, Agamben shows that the oath — an ancient attempt to guarantee that words will match deeds — was bound up from the very beginning with the possibility of breaking it. An oath is needed precisely because a word can turn out to be untrue. Following this line, betrayal is not proof of your naivety. Trust was always a risk, and you took it because there is no closeness without trust. The pain of betrayal is the price of that courage, not evidence of a mistake. Your capacity to trust is not broken — it is wounded, and it needs time.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud — to yourself or to someone you trust: “I trusted because…” — and finish the sentence. Hear that this trust was a brave act, not foolishness.

jealousy.text: “Mine” — the shortest word of jealousy. Studying the Franciscans, Agamben looked for a life in which that word does not exist. Jealousy is agonizing: love and the fear of loss are mixed in it. In The Highest Poverty, Agamben reflects on the Franciscans, who renounced property but not the use of things: living with things without owning them. He sees in this an image of a different relationship to the world — use without appropriation. In this light, jealousy is an attempt to turn love into property, to hold on to a person as a possession. But closeness, like Franciscan “poverty,” can be a bond without appropriation. This doesn’t mean giving up the feeling — it means asking what a love might be like that doesn’t hold on but shares.
jealousy.practice: Take a walk for a few minutes and look at what doesn’t belong to you but can still be used: the sky, a bench, someone’s garden over the fence. Notice that enjoying them doesn’t require owning them.

resentment.text: One of the first photographs ever, Daguerre’s Paris boulevard, froze forever a man having his boots shined: Agamben sees in such images the Last Judgment. Long-held resentment is heavy, and there is usually a real injustice behind it. The Coming Community has a short chapter called “Irreparable.” Agamben writes that things are as they are — delivered over to their way of being with no possibility of correction. He sees in it a source of liberation: acknowledging the irreparable frees us from the endless attempt to rewrite the past. It follows that resentment keeps an unfinished trial going inside — as if the past could still be put right if you remember the wrong long enough. Acknowledging that it was the way it was doesn’t mean justifying it. It means no longer spending your life on a trial that can never end.
resentment.practice: Say aloud: “It was the way it was” — and notice what changes in your body as you say it.

heartbreak.text: Could you ever have known the other person completely? Agamben answers: no — and that is not a misfortune but the very essence of love. When your heart is broken, it really hurts. In Idea of Prose, Agamben describes love as living in intimacy with something foreign — not in order to appropriate it or make it fully understandable, but to preserve its otherness. If we carry Agamben’s thought further, a breakup lays bare what was true before as well: the other person never fully belonged to you; they always remained themselves. That is bitter, but there is consolation in it too: what you loved was real precisely because it was other, not a copy of you. Your love was not a mistake — it was an encounter with someone other that changed you.
heartbreak.practice: Recall one habit or turn of phrase of this person that is nothing like yours, and silently thank them for that difference — for having been someone other.

impostor.text: Agamben describes a performance by Vanessa Beecroft in Berlin: a hundred almost naked women stand before a clothed audience — and nothing is revealed. The fear of being found out is exhausting, and you are far from alone in it. In the essay “Nudity,” he reflects on what we imagine lies beneath clothing — as if some secret were hidden there, a shameful truth. But for Agamben, being unclothed reveals nothing of the kind: behind the clothing there is no hidden essence, only a “this” — the body as it is. Agamben would probably say that impostor syndrome lives on the same fear: as if a shameful truth were hidden behind your work. But behind your deeds there is no secret “really, I’m nobody.” There is you — as you are, doing what you do. There is nothing to expose.
impostor.practice: Imagine you have been “found out,” and honestly play the scene to the end: what exactly did they see? Often it turns out to be simply a person who is learning and doing what they can.

self_hatred.text: Who said what you were supposed to become? Agamben suspects that no one did — and that this is exactly why you are free. If your inner voice says cruel things about you, that is very hard. In The Coming Community, in the short chapter on ethics, Agamben writes that there is no essence a human being must embody, no destiny they must fulfil. That is precisely why ethics is possible at all. It turns out that the inner critic compares you with an ideal that doesn’t actually exist — with the “right” you that you supposedly should have become. But there is no such standard. You haven’t failed your destiny, because there wasn’t one. You are a possibility, not a failed project.
self_hatred.practice: When your inner critic says its line, answer it aloud, calmly, like Bartleby: “I would prefer not to match a template that doesn’t exist.”

helplessness.text: An architect who is not building anything right now is still an architect: Aristotle argued this against the Megarians, and Agamben made the dispute one of the great themes of his life. When you can’t change anything, it is very hard, and it often reflects real circumstances. Agamben reflects a great deal on Aristotle’s thought that human potential always includes the potential not to: whoever can play the flute can also not play. Impotence, for Agamben, is not simply a lack of power but part of human potential. What matters to Agamben here is this: even when you can’t change your circumstances, you don’t turn into a thing: your capacity to choose your attitude, to notice, to wait remains. This is not a promise of change. It is a recognition that even in powerlessness you remain alive, not a broken mechanism.
helplessness.practice: Clench your hand and slowly open it. Then simply let it rest, unclenched. Notice: both “doing” and “not doing” are yours.

procrastination.text: A scrivener who one day stopped writing — Agamben considers him one of the most enigmatic figures in literature. “I can’t get started” is agonizing, and it isn’t laziness. In the essay “Bartleby, or On Contingency,” Agamben examines Herman Melville’s story about a scrivener who answers every request with: “I would prefer not to.” For Agamben, Bartleby is a figure of the “potential not to”: a person can not only do but also not do, and therein lies their freedom. It seems that procrastination is a spontaneous expression of this potential, which we experience as guilt. But it is important to ask: what exactly in me wants to say “I would prefer not to”? Sometimes it is a protest against the task, sometimes tiredness, sometimes fear. Once you hear it, it is easier to find where to begin.
procrastination.practice: Say, like Bartleby: “I would prefer not to…” — and finish what exactly. Then ask: and what would I prefer to do — the smallest thing?

quote.author: Herman Melville
quote.source: “Bartleby, the Scrivener” (Agamben devoted his essay “Bartleby, or On Contingency” to this phrase)

uprooted.text: Paroikia, “sojourning in a foreign land” — that is what the first Christians called their community, and Agamben reminds us that the word “parish” comes from it. Being cut off from home — losing your ground, your language, your familiar ties — is a profound experience. In the essay “Beyond Human Rights,” following Hannah Arendt, Agamben reflects on the figure of the person who has left their country. He suggests that this is not an exception to the rule but perhaps one of the central figures of our time: more and more people live between places and languages. In other words, you haven’t fallen out of normal life — you are living an experience that says a great deal about the modern world. His “coming community” is a community that doesn’t require a single shared soil. You can belong without being “from here.”
uprooted.practice: Call or send a few words to one person in your new place with whom you are connected not by origin but by something else. Just so the connection is heard.

overload.text: A traveller once brought home one story for a lifetime; now we come home with a hundred pieces of news and not a single story. Overload is real, and the endless feed really is draining. In Infancy and History, Agamben observes that modern people come home in the evening worn out by a multitude of events — and not one of them has become experience. We are flooded with impressions, but they don’t add up to anything lived through. In the essay “On What We Can Not Do,” he adds: we have lost touch with our “potential not to,” and so we believe we must cope with everything. Agamben might point out that your overload is not an inability but a sign that you have been deprived of the right not to take things in. Reclaiming your “not” means beginning to have experience again.
overload.practice: Switch off one notification for an hour and say the formula of the “potential not to”: “I can not know this right now.”

quote.text: Separated from his impotentiality, deprived of the experience of what he can not do, today’s man believes himself capable of everything.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben
quote.source: “On What We Can Not Do,” Nudities

unreality.text: Guy Debord, Agamben’s friend, wrote that everything once directly lived has moved away into a representation. When everything around feels not quite real, it is frightening and disorienting. Continuing Debord’s idea of “the society of the spectacle,” Agamben writes about a world in which reality increasingly turns into images and pictures, and language and experience are separated from us. Following this line, the sense of unreality partly echoes this era: you are not making it up out of nothing. But Agamben also sees a chance in it — to see what is usually hidden behind familiarity. Unreality can be gently balanced by what is simple and tangible, what can’t be turned into a picture.
unreality.practice: Touch three objects with different textures and slowly say aloud what each one feels like — something that can’t be turned into a picture.

awe.text: Why is the night sky dark if there are so many stars? Agamben starts one of his most beautiful pages with this astrophysicists’ question. Awe before something vast is a rare and precious state. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben offers an image that evokes exactly this feeling. The night sky is dark because the light of distant galaxies, moving away from us, travels toward us but cannot reach us. To see in the darkness this light that is striving toward us — that is what it means to be contemporary. In this light, awe is the experience of something that exceeds our capacity to take it in and yet touches us. It doesn’t need explaining. You can simply let yourself be the one the light reaches.
awe.practice: Look at the evening or night sky — or picture it — and for a minute be the one toward whom distant light is travelling. Explain nothing.

relief.text: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning,” Paul writes to the Corinthians. Relief, when something that pressed on you finally lets go, is worth living. In The Time That Remains, Agamben reads Paul’s “as not” — living in your roles and duties as though they don’t hold you entirely. The roles remain, but they lose their power over you. It follows that relief is the moment when one of these roles or duties suddenly loosens its grip: you are still the same person, but you no longer have to hold on to it with all your strength. You can savor relief and remember it as a reminder: not every burden has to rest on you forever.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly, let your shoulders drop, and name what you have just been freed from. Feel this “as not” pass through your body.

calm.text: When words stop conveying anything and simply sound, poetry begins — this is how Agamben describes one form of inoperativity. Calm is like that, and worth protecting. For Agamben, inoperativity (inoperosità) is neither emptiness nor laziness but a special state in which life is not subordinated to a task. In The Coming Community he also speaks of “ease” (Italian agio) — the free space beside a thing where it can move. If we carry Agamben’s thought further, calm is this kind of ease: you are doing nothing useful, yet living more fully. Calm doesn’t need to be turned into rest for the sake of new tasks. It is good in itself.
calm.practice: Read aloud, slowly, two lines of any poem you remember — not thinking about the meaning, only listening to how the words sound.

inspiration.text: Does the poet write, or does someone write through them? Agamben thinks the right answer is both. When you want to create, it is a joyful state. In the essay “Genius,” from Profanations, Agamben recalls that the ancient Romans believed each person has their own Genius — a god born together with them. For Agamben, Genius is the impersonal part of us, something greater than our “I” that doesn’t entirely belong to us. Agamben would probably say that inspiration is an encounter with this part. You don’t produce inspiration through effort; it comes as if you were living alongside someone strange and generous. You don’t need to appropriate or control it. You can simply follow it for as long as it leads.
inspiration.practice: Write down whatever comes, without editing — as if taking dictation from your Genius.

schadenfreude.text: Shop window, ranking, feed — following Guy Debord, Agamben sees in them the stage of a vast spectacle where everyone watches everyone. When someone’s failure suddenly pleases you, it is usually embarrassing, though it says little about you. He writes about a world in which life increasingly becomes a show: we watch other people’s successes and failures like images in a shop window, where everyone is constantly being compared. It turns out that schadenfreude is the feeling of a spectator at this spectacle. When someone else’s life becomes a picture in a ranking, their fall briefly lifts us a rung higher. Simply noticing that you have ended up in the role of spectator is already freeing: behind the picture a living person shows through again — and so does your own weariness with the race.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, ask yourself: what competition am I taking part in right now — and did I choose it?

contempt.text: Agamben opens The Open with a thirteenth-century Hebrew miniature: the righteous at the banquet at the end of time are shown with the heads of animals. Contempt is a cold look from above, and it often protects: against disappointment, powerlessness, fear. There he describes what he calls the “anthropological machine”: the way a culture again and again defines the “true human” by separating off those declared “lower,” almost animal. What matters to Agamben here is this: contempt is a small, personal version of this machine: it draws a line with “us” on one side and those who are beneath us on the other. Agamben proposes stopping the machine — not drawing a new line but suspending the division itself. You don’t need to force yourself to respect someone you despise. But you can notice the line you are drawing and ask what it protects in you.
contempt.practice: Picture for a minute the table from that miniature, where the line between “higher” and “lower” no longer holds, and seat yourself and this person at it. Notice what your line was protecting.

disgust.text: Is taste a kind of knowledge? Medieval thinkers argued about it, and Agamben devoted his book Taste to the question. Disgust is a very bodily feeling: the body recoils before thought does. He shows that taste is a special kind of knowledge: it doesn’t prove anything but distinguishes the pleasant from the unpleasant immediately, with the body. It seems that disgust is the dark side of this capacity: the body’s instant knowledge of what it doesn’t want to let in. It isn’t always right, but it always tells you something. If disgust is directed at yourself, it is worth recalling Agamben’s thought from The Coming Community: a person is not a sum of properties that can be taken away or rejected, but a way of being. What seems “vile” in you is not the whole truth about you.
disgust.practice: Breathe out slowly, as if releasing what your body is recoiling from, and name it in one word. Ask: is this knowledge about the world, or about my tiredness?

revenge.text: An eye for an eye is the oldest bookkeeping in the world, and Agamben asks whether ethics must obey it. The wish for revenge speaks to the depth of the wound and doesn’t make you cruel. In his short book Karman, Agamben explores how Western thought linked action, guilt and punishment into a single chain: every act gives rise to a debt that must be paid. He doubts that this bookkeeping exhausts ethics. In other words, revenge lives by the same logic: the account stays open until the pain has been returned. But such a chain rarely ends — it only passes from one person to the next. Acknowledging your wish for revenge is honest. Asking what would really give you back your footing means stepping out of the bookkeeping, without giving up on justice or on protecting yourself.
revenge.practice: Walk for a few minutes and, every tenth step, set aside one item from the “account” in your mind. At the end ask: what would really give me back my footing?

anger_at_loved.text: You can’t hug an icon or quarrel with it — and Agamben notices we sometimes treat those we love that way. Anger at a partner, parents, children can be sharp, and then shame arrives, but it doesn’t cancel love. In “In Praise of Profanation,” Agamben writes that everything declared sacred is removed from ordinary life: it can’t be touched, it can’t be freely used. Agamben might point out that family roles, too, sometimes become such “sacred” images: the perfect mother, the grateful son, the flawless partner. They are not allowed to be angry or tired. Anger at someone close is sometimes a clumsy profanation of these roles: a return of the relationship to ordinary, living, imperfect life. This is no reason to hurt the people you love. But it is a reason to forgive yourself for being a living person and not an icon.
anger_at_loved.practice: Tell someone close one plain, un-iconic sentence about yourself: “I’m tired today” or “That hurt me.” Let the relationship be ordinary for a minute.

ambivalence.text: Must you choose between “yes” and “no”? All his life Agamben has defended a third possibility — “I can, and I can not.” Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a tangled feeling. Agamben reflects a great deal on Aristotle’s thought that every potential is at once a potential to be and a potential not to be, to do and not to do. One doesn’t exist without the other. Following this line, closeness works the same way: the capacity to love someone is inseparable from the capacity to pull away, be irritated, disagree. Ambivalence is not a breakdown of love but a sign that it is alive and free rather than compelled. A love without the possibility of “not” would be more like a duty. You can let both feelings be, without demanding an immediate choice of yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Say quietly: “I can love you and I can not stand you — and both are mine.” Stay with this sentence for a minute.

guilty_relief.text: A priest says Mass because it is his office, not because he wants to: Agamben sees here the whole ethics of duty. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a seriously ill loved one often comes with shame, though it can live beside love. In Opus Dei, Agamben traces how the notion of duty, of service, of “office” gradually became the main model of ethics: to live is to carry out an obligation. In this light, long care for a loved one or a hard relationship turns life into just such an endless service, with no room for anything but the function. Relief is the moment when the service is over and life can once again simply be life. This doesn’t cancel the love that was inside that service. Your relief is not a betrayal but a release from a burden you carried because you loved.
guilty_relief.practice: Put your hand on your heart and say: “My service is over, and the love remains.” Notice what happens in your body.

indifference.text: Agamben’s first book opens with Nietzsche’s complaint against Kant: beauty “without interest” is a spectator’s view, not an artist’s. Sometimes something “should” move you, yet inside it is quiet — and you wonder: “Am I heartless?” In that book, The Man Without Content, Agamben reflects on the modern spectator: more and more, we look at the world from the outside, as if at an exhibition, and precisely for that reason it less and less truly grips us. In Infancy and History he adds that modern people live through many events that never become experience. It follows that your indifference is not a personal flaw but a shared affliction of an era that buries us in impressions and robs us of the time to live through them. Your feelings haven’t disappeared — they simply had nowhere to enter. Perhaps they need quiet and slowing down.
indifference.practice: Choose one event from the past few days and stay with it for two minutes not as a spectator but as a participant: no phone, just returning to the details.

escape.text: In 2004 Agamben refused to lecture in the United States because the border demanded fingerprints. The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — can be very strong: this is often how something speaks that has long been given no room. In the essay “What Is an Apparatus?”, Agamben describes how modern life is saturated with apparatuses — schedules, rules, positions, gadgets — that capture our gestures and desires. He notes that you can’t simply run away from apparatuses: new ones appear everywhere. But you can “profane” them — take back free use of what has been captured. If we carry Agamben’s thought further, the wish to run away is a sign that you have felt this capture. Whether to leave or not is for you alone to decide. But first you can notice which part of your life you want to take back, wherever you end up.
escape.practice: For five minutes, walk a different way than usual — somewhere you never turn. Notice what of what has been captured you can take back even on such a short walk.

forbidden_attraction.text: Narcissus falls in love not with a person but with a reflection — and in Stanzas Agamben shows that medieval poets saw this myth as the model of all love. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” often brings turmoil, as if the feeling itself were a transgression, though it says little about your integrity. There Agamben examines the medieval theory of love, according to which one loves not simply a person but their image — a “phantasm” that the imagination keeps and cherishes within. The poets of that time knew that love largely converses with this inner image. Agamben would probably say that attraction to someone unavailable is often especially strong precisely because the image has no limits: reality doesn’t argue with it. That doesn’t make the feeling false. But you can ask with curiosity: what exactly lives in this image — and what does it say about you yourself?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Close your eyes and describe to yourself, in three words, the image of this person that lives in your imagination. Ask: what does this image want in me?

social_anxiety.text: Where do you put your face when everyone is looking? Agamben would answer: nowhere — and there is no harm in that. Fear of people and their judgment — the stiffness, the burning cheeks, the wish to become invisible — is exhausting, and you are not alone in it. In the short essay “The Face,” Agamben writes that the face is above all openness: the place where a person is exposed to others and cannot escape it. We all try to cope with this exposure — we hide behind roles, masks, expressions. It turns out that social anxiety is an acute experience of this shared openness. But it isn’t peculiar to you: everyone in the room is just as exposed, just as vulnerable. Agamben even saw in this shared openness a basis for human community. Your vulnerability is not a defect but the very thing that connects you with others.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, take one slow breath out and tell yourself: “Everyone here is just as open as I am.”

uncertainty.text: Will there be a sea battle tomorrow? Agamben recalls this question of Aristotle’s when he thinks about the contingent. Not knowing what will happen is hard: the mind tries again and again to calculate everything. Agamben thinks a great deal about the “contingent” in the old philosophical sense: contingent is what can be and can also not be. We are used to seeing a threat in this. But for Agamben, contingency is the condition of freedom: in a world where everything was necessary and predetermined, there would be no room for either choice or hope. What matters to Agamben here is this: uncertainty is a world in which possibility is still at work. That doesn’t cancel the anxiety: not knowing is hard. But you can remember that an open future is not only a space of bad outcomes. It also holds ones you haven’t thought of yet.
uncertainty.practice: Picture your own “sea battle” tomorrow in two versions, then add a third — one you haven’t thought of yet and that would make you glad.

waiting.text: “The Messiah will come not on the last day, but on the very last,” Kafka wrote, and Agamben often returns to the line. When you are waiting for an answer, results, news, time stretches out, and life seems to be put on pause. In The Time That Remains, Agamben reads the apostle Paul and speaks of “messianic time.” It is not a distant end to be waited out but a time within time: a special, contracted “now” in which we already live. For Agamben, what matters in it is not what comes afterward but how we live this interval. It seems that waiting is not empty time that you simply have to endure. Even when the outcome isn’t in your hands, the interval belongs to you. You can live it, not just sit it out.
waiting.practice: For two minutes set aside thoughts of the outcome and look out of the window as if this interval were the time that matters most: what is happening outside right now?

quote.text: Messianic time is the time that time takes to come to an end.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

regret.text: Everything that was could have been otherwise — Agamben considers this simple thought one of the most liberating. Regret can keep coming back for years: “if only I had…” — and it shows what mattered to you. In the essay “Bartleby, or On Contingency,” Agamben recalls a thought of Walter Benjamin’s: remembrance can make the incomplete complete, and the complete incomplete. For Agamben, memory doesn’t simply store the past; it gives it back its possibility: what was opens up anew — as something that could have been otherwise. In other words, regret is a painful form of this kind of memory: you see possibilities in the past that were never realized. They can’t be brought back, but they can be acknowledged. Sometimes what didn’t happen then can find another, new place in your life now.
regret.practice: Picture the missed possibility as a seed that didn’t sprout back then. Where in your life now could it find a place — even the smallest?

longing.text: A servant girl in Ghirlandaio’s Florentine fresco enters the room with a quick step, her dress still fluttering: Warburg called her the Nymph, and Agamben saw in her an image that goes on living. Missing the voice, the gaze, the presence of a particular person can be almost physical pain. In Nymphs, Agamben writes about the “afterlife” of images: images are not dead; they are charged with time and go on living, returning, stirring us. Agamben might point out that the image of someone you love within you is not a pale copy but a living, charged image: it comes in dreams, in the chance gestures of passers-by, in smells. Longing is an encounter with such an image when the person themselves is not near. It hurts, but it also keeps the connection. You don’t have to fight this image; you can let it live in you.
longing.practice: Let yourself remember this person for a minute in one scene, in motion, as in the fresco — with its light, sounds and details.

world_pain.text: Latin has two words for a witness, Agamben notes, and one of them, superstes, means “the one who lived through it and remained.” When hard news, wars and injustice overwhelm you so much that it is hard to live your own life, it hurts a great deal. In Remnants of Auschwitz, Agamben reflects on testimony: on how hard and how important it is to listen to those who have survived terrible things, and not to turn away from the unbearable. He writes that complete testimony is impossible: the most terrible things always remain unspoken. Following this line, your pain is a form of bearing witness: you don’t look away. But a witness doesn’t have to bear everything alone. You can listen, remember, name — and still give yourself pauses. Being faithful to the world doesn’t require you to be destroyed along with it.
world_pain.practice: Choose one thing you want to remember from what you saw today and say it aloud in one sentence, as a witness. Then put the news aside and do something caring for yourself.

rejection.text: Imagine that everyone always said “yes” to you. Agamben would point out that such a “yes” would be worth nothing. Rejection wounds painfully: it feels as though a verdict has been passed on you. Following Aristotle, Agamben says that every potential includes the “potential not to”: whoever can do something can also not do it. In this possibility of refusal he sees the essence of human freedom. In this light, another person’s “no” is an expression of their freedom, their “potential not to,” and not a measure of your worth. They could have said “yes,” they could have said “no” — and they chose “no” for their own reasons, which are not always about you. In The Coming Community, Agamben insists that a person is valuable not for a set of properties someone has approved or rejected, but for their very way of being.
rejection.practice: Read aloud, slowly: “Their ‘no’ is about their freedom. My worth hasn’t changed because of it.”

abandonment.text: Medieval theologians argued about the children in limbo, forgotten by God — and Agamben writes tenderly that these forgotten ones are not unhappy at all: they live in their natural joy. The fear of being abandoned can be tenacious, and behind it is a real need for a secure connection. In The Coming Community, he dreams of a community that doesn’t require a person to earn belonging, meet conditions, or prove they are “one of us.” It follows that the fear of abandonment often lives by the logic of conditions: “they’ll leave me if I turn out not to be enough…” Agamben proposes seeing a person as “whatever” being — valuable not for meeting requirements but simply as it is. This doesn’t guarantee that no one will ever leave. But it reminds you: your worth doesn’t depend on whether people stay with you.
abandonment.practice: Send someone close a short, warm message for no reason — and don’t check whether they have replied. Let the connection be a gift, not a condition.

unrequited.text: The troubadours sang of ladies who never answered them — and Agamben notes that all of European lyric poetry grew out of this unanswered love. When the feeling is enormous and there is no answer, it hurts in a special way. In Stanzas, Agamben explains that the Italian word stanza means “dwelling,” “room”: poets used it for the essential part of a poem, which holds love like a home. Medieval love poetry was often born of love that received no answer — and it was this poetry that created such “rooms” for it. If we carry Agamben’s thought further, unrequited love is not wasted: it needs a place where it can live without demanding an answer. That place can be a letter, poems, a diary, music, or simply an inner room. You can grieve what didn’t come true — and still give your feeling a home rather than driving it out.
unrequited.practice: Write a few lines about your love, without addressing the person and without planning to send them. Let it have a “room” of its own.

humiliation.text: The Roman theatre called its mask persona, and Agamben reminds us that our word “person” comes from it. Losing your place among people is one of the most painful experiences, and the blame is not yours. In Remnants of Auschwitz, Agamben points out that the Latin dignitas — “dignity” — originally meant rank, office, standing in society. Dignity of this kind can be taken away, the way someone is removed from office. Agamben would probably say that humiliation strikes precisely at this “dignity as rank”: at the place others assign to you. But a person does not coincide with their role and mask. In The Coming Community, Agamben speaks of the human being as a way of being that can’t be reduced to a position or an assessment. Humiliation wounds — but what in you runs deeper than any role cannot be taken from you.
humiliation.practice: Straighten your back, put your feet on the floor and feel that the support beneath you hasn’t gone anywhere. Name one thing in you that doesn’t depend on anyone else’s gaze.

body_shame.text: Whom does your body belong to — you, the mirror, or the market? Agamben offers an answer that has no “belong” in it. Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background, and behind it lies real pressure — advertising, comparisons, other people’s remarks. In his late book The Use of Bodies, Agamben proposes thinking of the body not as property to be appraised like an item on the market but through “use”: a living relationship in which we not only use the body but are ourselves affected by it. It turns out that body shame arises when the body turns into a shop window, an object to be judged from outside. In use, the body is what you live with: you walk, embrace, taste food, feel warmth. You may not love every feature and still give your body back its life — from the inside, not from the mirror.
body_shame.practice: Walk around the room for a minute without looking in the mirror, noticing how your body lives from the inside: feet, knees, breath, the warmth of your hands.

illness.text: Hölderlin spent his last thirty-six years in a Tübingen carpenter’s tower, and Agamben saw in them not a collapse but another form of life. When your body lets you down, it is frightening and painful, and you seem reduced to a diagnosis. Agamben speaks of “form-of-life” — a life that cannot be separated from its form: from its way of living, feeling, looking at the world. He criticizes the habit of dividing a person into “bare” biological life and everything else. What matters to Agamben here is this: even in illness you are not just an organism with symptoms but a whole form of life: your attachments, habits, your way of seeing. Illness changes this form but doesn’t cancel it. You can take care of your body and at the same time protect what makes your life yours — small things, conversations, things you love.
illness.practice: Talk with someone close for five minutes about anything but the illness: a book, the weather, a shared memory. Let it be part of your form of life.

pride.text: In The Kingdom and the Glory, Agamben shows how for centuries power has needed praise, hymns and applause. Pride in what you have done needs none of that: it is a good, well-earned feeling, and there is no need to hide it. In Infancy and History, Agamben writes that modern people live through many events but rarely a real experience: something truly lived, understood and made their own. It seems that healthy pride is a rare moment of exactly this kind of experience. You did something, and it isn’t just an item on a to-do list — it has become part of you. Agamben also values the “potential not to”: part of your pride may also be about what you managed to turn down in order to do what mattered most. You can let yourself be fully glad, without rushing on to the next task.
pride.practice: Tell someone close, or yourself aloud, the story of what you did in three sentences: the beginning, the difficulty, the result. No modest disclaimers.

melancholy.text: A grindstone, scales, an hourglass, a sleeping dog — everything lies idle around the winged figure in Dürer’s engraving. A bright sadness is a quiet, slightly sad and yet warm state, and it doesn’t need fixing. In Stanzas, Agamben examines Albrecht Dürer’s engraving Melencolia I in detail, where objects have lost their usual purpose. For Agamben, the melancholy gaze sees things differently: not as means to an end but as if for the first time — in their strangeness and beauty. It is no accident that melancholy has long been associated with contemplation and creativity. A bright sadness lets you see the familiar as precious and fragile. You can simply stay in it for a while, letting the things around you become a little more meaningful.
melancholy.practice: Choose an object near you and look at it for a minute as if it weren’t needed for anything — as if it simply is.
